learn: You can start counting from any number, not just one.
Starting at 47, count on: 48, 49, 50, 51.
Counting on helps you add and find what comes next.
check: Start at 67 and count on two. Where do you land?
lessons.try: Start at 85 and count on to 100.

learn: After 100 comes 101, 102, 103 and so on.
The pattern is the same as 1, 2, 3, just with 100 in front.
We count all the way to 120.
lessons.try: Count from 100 to 120 out loud.

learn: Numbers can be written with digits: 73.
The number 73 is read "seventy-three".
A hundred chart helps you see number patterns: each row goes up by ten.
check: On a hundred chart, each row goes up by...
lessons.try: Write the numbers 95 to 105.

learn: Ten ones can be bundled into one ten.
10 straws tied together make a ten.
Bundling tens makes big numbers easier to count.
lessons.try: Bundle 30 sticks or straws into tens. How many bundles?

learn: A two-digit number has a tens place and a ones place.
In 46, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 6 means 6 ones.
lessons.try: Show 35 with 3 bundles of ten and 5 single sticks.

learn: Numbers like 10, 20, 30 up to 90 have zero ones.
70 is 7 tens and 0 ones.
lessons.try: Count by tens to 100 while clapping.

learn: To compare two numbers, look at the tens first.
52 is greater than 38 because 5 tens is more than 3 tens.
If the tens are the same, look at the ones: 47 is greater than 43.
check: What do you look at first?
lessons.try: Compare 61 and 59. Which is greater?

learn: The symbol > means greater than. The symbol < means less than. The symbol = means equal.
The open side faces the bigger number, like a hungry mouth.
lessons.try: Write <, > or = for 33 and 35.

learn: To order numbers, compare them one at a time.
From least to greatest: 18, 41, 67, 90.
A number line shows smaller numbers to the left and bigger to the right.
check: On a number line, bigger numbers are to the...
lessons.try: Order 55, 12, 87 and 34 from least to greatest.

learn: To add, start with the bigger number and count on.
For 8 + 3, start at 8 and count 9, 10, 11. So 8 + 3 = 11.
The order does not change the sum: 3 + 8 = 8 + 3.
lessons.try: Add 9 + 4 by counting on.

learn: Breaking a number to make a ten is a fast strategy.
8 + 5: take 2 from the 5 to make 8 into 10. Then 10 + 3 = 13.
10 plus a number is easy: 10 + 6 = 16.
lessons.try: Solve 7 + 6 by making a ten.

learn: Doubles are adding a number to itself: 6 + 6 = 12.
Near doubles are one more: 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 + 1 = 13.
Knowing doubles makes adding faster.
lessons.try: Say all the doubles from 1 + 1 to 10 + 10.

learn: Subtracting means taking some away to find how many are left.
12 - 4: start with 12, take away 4, and 8 are left.
The answer to a subtraction is called the difference.
check: The answer to a subtraction is the...
lessons.try: Put out 14 buttons and take 6 away. How many are left?

learn: Addition and subtraction are related.
To solve 13 - 5, think: 5 plus what makes 13? 5 + 8 = 13, so 13 - 5 = 8.
A fact family uses the same three numbers: 5 + 8 = 13, 8 + 5 = 13, 13 - 5 = 8, 13 - 8 = 5.
check: Which is in the same fact family as 6 + 9 = 15?
lessons.try: Write the fact family for 4, 7 and 11.

learn: For small take-aways, count back.
15 - 3: start at 15 and count back 14, 13, 12. So the answer is 12.
Subtracting 0 leaves the number the same: 9 - 0 = 9.
lessons.try: Count back to solve 17 - 2.

units.t: Word Problems and the Equal Sign

learn: A word problem tells a math story.
Read it, find the numbers and decide: are things joining (add) or leaving (subtract)?
"Sam has 7 apples. He gets 5 more. How many now?" 7 + 5 = 12.
check: Sam has 7 apples and gets 5 more. How many now?
10 birds sit. 3 fly away. How many are left?
lessons.try: Make up a story for 9 - 4.

learn: You can add three numbers.
Look for two that make ten first: 4 + 6 + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13.
You can add in any order.
check: Can you add three numbers in any order?
lessons.try: Add 5 + 2 + 5 by finding the ten.

learn: The equal sign means both sides have the same value.
6 + 2 = 8 is true. 8 = 5 + 3 is also true.
4 + 4 = 5 + 3 is true because both sides make 8.
lessons.try: Is 7 = 3 + 3 true or false?

learn: Adding tens is like adding ones, but with tens.
3 tens + 2 tens = 5 tens. So 30 + 20 = 50.
10 more than a number: the tens go up by one. 10 more than 34 is 44.
lessons.try: Find 10 more and 10 less than 56.

learn: 23 + 40: add the tens. 2 tens + 4 tens = 6 tens. The 3 ones stay. 63.
The ones digit does not change when you add only tens.
A hundred chart helps: jump down one row for each ten.
check: When you add only tens, the ones digit...
lessons.try: Solve 45 + 30 on a hundred chart.

lessons.t: Adding a Two-Digit and One-Digit Number
learn: 34 + 5: add the ones. 4 + 5 = 9, so 39.
36 + 7: 6 + 7 = 13 ones, which is 1 ten and 3 ones. 3 tens + 1 ten = 4 tens. So 43.
When ones make ten or more, make a new ten.
lessons.try: Solve 28 + 6 with sticks.

learn: Length is how long something is.
To compare, line up the ends: the one that sticks out is longer.
If A is longer than B, and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C.
check: To compare length you line up...
A is longer than B, B longer than C. Which is longest?
lessons.try: Put three pencils in order from shortest to longest.

learn: You can measure with paper clips or cubes laid end to end.
No gaps and no overlaps.
The number of units is the length: the book is 8 paper clips long.
check: A book is 8 clips long. Its length is...
Which can be used to measure?
lessons.try: Measure your shoe in paper clips.

learn: A clock has an hour hand (short) and a minute hand (long).
When the minute hand points to 12, it is o'clock: 3:00.
When the minute hand points to 6, it is half past: 3:30.
check: Minute hand on 12 and hour hand on 3 is...
lessons.try: Look at a clock at home at a time that is o'clock or half past.

learn: To sort is to put things into groups that are alike.
You can sort by colour, size or shape.
Sorting helps us count and compare.
lessons.try: Sort a handful of coins or buttons in two different ways.

learn: Tally marks are lines that count: four lines and a slash across make 5.
A picture graph uses pictures to show how many.
Each picture can stand for one thing.
check: A bundle of tally marks with a slash means...
lessons.try: Make a tally of the colours of cars you see.

learn: A bar graph shows how many with bars.
The tallest bar shows the most. The shortest shows the least.
You can ask: how many more? If cats got 7 votes and dogs got 4, cats got 3 more.
check: Cats 7, dogs 4. How many more for cats?
lessons.try: Ask your family their favourite fruit and make a bar graph.

learn: Shapes are named by their sides and corners (vertices).
A triangle has 3 sides. A square and a rectangle have 4. A hexagon has 6.
Colour and size do not change the shape's name.
check: How many sides does a hexagon have?
Does colour change a shape's name?
A shape with 3 sides is a...
lessons.try: Find a shape with 4 sides and one with 3 sides at home.

learn: Solid shapes are 3D: cube, cone, cylinder, sphere.
A ball is a sphere. A can is a cylinder.
You can put shapes together to make new shapes: two triangles can make a square.
lessons.try: Use blocks to build a new shape from two smaller ones.

learn: Equal parts are the same size.
Two equal parts are halves. Four equal parts are fourths, also called quarters.
More equal parts means each part is smaller.
check: Which is smaller: a half or a fourth of the same pizza?
lessons.try: Fold a paper square into halves, then into fourths.
